summary: Describes YANG data models for configuring and managing DHCPv6 servers, relays, and clients, building on the DHCPv6 protocol in RFC 8415. A YANG model lets network management tools set up and monitor these components in a consistent, machine-readable way. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: DHCPv6 hands out network addresses, a bit like a hotel desk handing out room keys. This gives the managers one standard form to set up and check the desk, no matter who made the software.

subtitle: Standard YANG modules for configuring and monitoring DHCPv6 servers, relays and clients over NETCONF or RESTCONF.

tldr.problem: Every DHCPv6 server, relay and client had its own way of being configured and monitored, so network management tools could not treat them the same way.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines four YANG modules (common, server, relay and client) that describe the configuration and state of each DHCPv6 element, to be used over NETCONF or RESTCONF.
tldr.outcome: Operators get one machine-readable model for the DHCPv6 functions in RFC 8415, with defined places to add vendor-specific settings, extra options and client classification.

facts.label: DUID
facts.value: 2-octet type plus content of up to 128 octets

today: RFC 9243 is a Standards Track document published in June 2022. It has not been obsoleted or updated, and it models only the DHCPv6 functions and options of RFC 8415. Appendix B says that additional specifications for further options are expected.

sections.title: What the Modules Are For
sections.content:
DHCPv6 (RFC 8415) supplies configuration and other parameters to clients in IPv6 networks. This RFC defines YANG modules for configuring and managing DHCPv6 elements: servers, relays and clients. The modules are meant to be used with the Network Configuration Protocol (NETCONF, RFC 6241) or RESTCONF (RFC 8040).

There is one module per element, plus a common module holding typedefs and groupings shared by all of them. The relay and client modules attach their settings to interfaces by importing the ietf-interfaces module (RFC 8343) and pointing at the relevant interfaces. The modules follow the Network Management Datastore Architecture (NMDA, RFC 8342).

The RFC is explicit that this is not a replacement for DHCPv6 itself. The client module configures and monitors the client function. It does not replace the way DHCPv6 hands out addresses and parameters.
sections.eli5: Think of a standard control panel for a machine. The same panel works whether the machine is the desk that gives out keys, the helper that passes requests along, or the guest asking for a key.

sections.title: Scope and Which Options Are Modeled
sections.content:
Many specifications have extended DHCPv6 since RFC 8415. The modules here do not try to capture them. They model only the DHCPv6 functions and options covered in RFC 8415, and are built so that other documents can augment them.

Even among the RFC 8415 options, only those that need operator configuration are modeled. For example, OPTION_IA_NA (3) is created by the server when a client asks, using inputs such as the T1/T2 timers for the address pool. It has no directly configurable fields, so it is left out.

The modeled options include the Option Request option (6), Preference (7), Authentication (11), Server Unicast (12), Rapid Commit (14), User Class (15), Vendor Class (16), Vendor-specific Information (17), Interface-Id (18), Reconfigure Message (19), Reconfigure Accept (20), Information Refresh Time (32), SOL_MAX_RT (82) and INF_MAX_RT (83). Each is placed in the server, relay or client module, or in the common module when more than one element uses it.
sections.eli5: The form only has boxes for things a person actually needs to fill in. Things the machine works out on its own do not get a box.

sections.title: The Server, Relay and Client Models
sections.content:
The server module has a top-level dhcpv6-server container with an enabled switch, the server DUID, reusable option-sets, and a hierarchy of allocation-ranges. Global settings such as lifetimes, renew and rebind times and rapid commit can be set at the top and overridden at each lower level. An allocation-range holds an IPv6 prefix, with address-pools (for IA_NA and IA_TA) and prefix-pools (for prefix delegation) below it. Pools can carry host reservations and read-only active-leases state. A statistics container counts messages by type.

The relay module has a relay-if list, one entry per client-facing interface. Each entry sets destination-address values (unicast or multicast), the link-address put into Relay-Forward messages, relay options (authentication and Interface-Id), statistics, and optionally read-only delegated prefix leases.

The client module has a client-if list with options the client sends (such as the Option Request list, Rapid Commit, User Class and Vendor Class), plus ia-na, ia-ta and ia-pd lists for the kinds of leases requested, each with read-only lease-state. Stateless DHCP is configured when all the address and prefix features are disabled.

Features keep the models honest about what an implementation supports. For example, prefix delegation is enabled through a feature statement because not every server or relay supports it.
sections.eli5: The server has a big binder with pages for each neighborhood and each pile of keys. The helper has one page per door it watches. The guest has one page for each kind of key it asks for.

sections.title: Actions and Notifications
sections.content:
Beyond configuration and read-only state, the modules define operations and events.

  • Server RPCs: delete-address-lease and delete-prefix-lease remove a single lease from the server's lease database.
  • Relay RPCs: clear-prefix-entry, clear-client-prefixes and clear-interface-prefixes remove delegated lease entries by prefix, by client DUID or by interface. These come from the requirements in RFC 8987.
  • Server notifications: address-pool-utilization-threshold-exceeded, prefix-pool-utilization-threshold-exceeded, invalid-client-detected, decline-received and non-success-code-sent.
  • Relay notification: relay-event, with a topology-change report when, for example, a client-facing interface is reconfigured.
  • Client notifications: invalid-ia-address-detected, transmission-failed, unsuccessful-status-code and server-duid-changed.

Pool utilization thresholds are expressed as a percentage. The common module defines the threshold type with a range of 1 to 100.
sections.eli5: Besides filling in forms, managers can press buttons like erase this one key. The machines can also ring a bell, for instance when the key pile is nearly empty.

sections.title: Extending the Modules
sections.content:
The RFC deliberately leaves two things out of the standard server module and shows how to add them with YANG augmentation.

Vendor-specific configuration. Server implementations vary too much to standardize, so a vendor-config container is provided as a hook. Appendix C gives an example module that configures where leases are stored, with memory, MySQL and PostgreSQL as the three choices.

Class selection. Servers commonly classify incoming messages (to choose a pool or a vendor-specific option set), but the researched implementations configure this in very different ways. A class-selector container is provided instead, and Appendix D shows one possible design that matches on things like client ID, interface ID, addresses or relay link address.

More options. New DHCPv6 options can be added through additional modules that augment the element modules. Appendix B shows this for the two SIP server options in RFC 3319, together with naming conventions: a grouping per option, named after the IANA option name with an -option suffix.
sections.eli5: The form has a blank page labeled Extras. Each company can add its own questions there without tearing up the standard form.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The modules are meant to be reached over NETCONF or RESTCONF. NETCONF's mandatory-to-implement secure transport is SSH, and RESTCONF's is TLS. The Network Configuration Access Control Model (NACM, RFC 8341) can limit which users see or change which nodes.

The RFC lists what writable nodes can be abused for:

  • Disabling the server or removing pools (denial of service).
  • Changing option contents, for example pointing a DNS server option at a rogue server.
  • On a relay, disabling it, pointing its destination address at a non-existent address (denial of service), or pointing it at a rogue DHCPv6 server.

The relay RPCs that clear leases use nacm:default-deny-all, since clearing active leases can cut clients off. An attacker who triggers many invalid-client-detected or decline-received notifications could cause a denial of service, which a NETCONF client can mitigate by unsubscribing from them.

Readable data can also be sensitive. Lease information can be used to track activity or fingerprint a host, and pool prefixes can help network reconnaissance (RFC 7707). The client module's anon-profile feature supports the anonymity profiles of RFC 7844, and RFC 7824 covers DHCPv6 privacy.
sections.eli5: If a stranger could edit the form, they could send guests to a fake desk or lock everyone out. So only trusted people get the pen, and some pages are kept private.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA registered four XML namespace URIs, one per module, in the IETF XML Registry. They have the form urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:yang:ietf-dhcpv6-server, with -relay, -client and -common for the other three. The four modules were also added to the YANG Module Names registry, with the prefixes dhc6-srv, dhc6-rly, dhc6-clnt and dhc6.
sections.eli5: Each of the four forms got its own official name in a big registry book, so nobody mixes them up.
